tagline: From Plateau Creek’s canyon to forests and lakes on a basalt cap.
intro: The Grand Mesa byway climbs from Plateau Creek’s canyon into evergreen forest, crossing the mesa between the towns of Mesa and Cedaredge. CDOT gives the route 63 miles and two hours, and highlights fishing, hiking and mountain biking among its attractions. The U.S. Secretary of Transportation designated it a National Scenic Byway in 1996. The highway and its Land’s End spur form the byway: one crosses the mesa, while the other reaches the observatory on its rim.

Part of the road story lies on the spur to Land’s End. During the Depression, 200 unemployed World War I veterans completed 9.2 miles of Land’s End Road between June 1933 and May 1934, earning a dollar a day. The Forest Service and Works Progress Administration built the observatory in 1936–37, with help from two Civilian Conservation Corps side camps.

Starting at I-70, follow Plateau Creek’s canyon toward Mesa, then climb the steep north side near Powderhorn. The forested top holds more than 300 lakes, including reservoirs for drinking water and irrigation. Highway 65 passes Island Lake in Grand Mesa National Forest. Land’s End is a separate spur west of Highway 65; the main crossing descends to Cedaredge below the southern slopes.

moments.title: Grand Mesa
moments.text: River cobbles beneath Grand Mesa’s basalt cap reveal a reversal: this high ground was once a valley. At least 27 lava flows formed the cap between about 10.9 and 9.6 million years ago. The hard basalt resisted erosion while the Colorado and Gunnison rivers cut down through surrounding sedimentary rocks. More than 300 lakes now dot the top, many serving as drinking-water and irrigation reservoirs. CDOT lists rainbow, cutthroat and brook trout among their fish. Beneath the basalt lie shale and sandstone. Farther down, the Mesaverde Group forms a cliff about halfway up the mesa’s side.

moments.title: Land's End Observatory
moments.text: The observatory’s walls and terrace use basalt selected from the mesa and fitted together. Built in 1936–37 by the Forest Service and Works Progress Administration, the ranger observatory stands on Grand Mesa’s rim. The road had already employed 200 World War I veterans during the Depression; they finished 9.2 miles in 1933–34 for a dollar a day. The veterans lived in army tents below the rim. Civil Service machine operators and Forest Service hires completed the road’s toughest stretch over the next two summers. Outside the building, a large viewing area overlooks western Colorado and eastern Utah.
moments.notice: The walls and terrace are built from basalt gathered on the mesa.

moments.title: Cedaredge
moments.text: Below Grand Mesa’s southern slopes, Cedaredge occupies the Surface Creek Valley, with views south to the San Juan Mountains. Its agriculture includes beef cattle, elk, apples and peaches. At Pioneer Town, the octagonal Bar-I Silos survive from a cattle ranch established in the early 1880s. The museum village’s saloon, bank and other early-20th-century town buildings are replicas. The silos are the ranch’s last remaining structures; the recreated village also includes a creamery and a working blacksmith’s shop. The harvest festival took the name AppleFest in 1978 and continues as a celebration of apples, arts, music and food.

practical: Land's End Observatory: Land’s End Road is about half paved and half gravel. The saved account reports the observatory building closed and boarded up as of 2022. (checked 2026-10-11)
